new_statements.rule_in_words: Dutch has word stress (p. 96: 'Dutch is a language with word stress'). Main stress in underived words and non-natively derived words is assigned right-to-left inside a window of the last two syllables (three under extrametricality) and correlates with the segmental shape of the final syllables: vowel-final words take penultimate stress (olie, kanarie); words ending in VVC, VCC or a diphthong(+C) take final stress (kanaal, perkament, kopij, paradijs); words ending in short vowel + one consonant take penultimate or antepenultimate stress because a final -VC syllable is made extrametrical by rule (13), and the antepenult cannot be reached when the penult is closed or contains a diphthong (Kager 1989: 227). Formalised as Main Stress Rule (11): build one left-dominant (trochaic) foot from the right edge whose weak position may not be a closed syllable or a diphthong, otherwise a monosyllabic foot, then mark it as the main stress. A schwa-headed syllable never bears any stress (4). Booij adds that stress is 'not completely unpredictable' but 'many cases of unpredictable stress will remain' (p. 100: minimal pairs kanon 'gun' v. kanon 'canon', servies v. Servisch; -ie words split olie/kanarie v. alibi v. melodie), historically a mixture of a Germanic initial, a French final and a Latin penult/antepenult pattern (p. 99), and he explicitly declines a syllable-weight interpretation of the MSR (fn. 8, p. 101: 'I do not give a weight interpretation to the MSR: it only establishes a correlation between main-stress locus and segmental make-up of words and syllables'), against Kager (1989).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 97: 'Secondary stress is determined by a rhythmic principle, that is, it creates an alternation of stressed and unstressed syllables' (automaat: main stress final, secondary initial; dominee the reverse); p. 99 (5) Optimal Grid Principle 'A prosodic word has an alternating stress pattern', restricted by (4) the Schwa Restriction; sec. 5.2.1 pp. 105-106: the Optimal Grid Rule applies after main stress and builds binary left-dominant feet; where perfect alternation is impossible the word-initial syllable takes the secondary stress (fonologie: secondary on fo-, not -no-): 'Dutch prefers stresses at (prosodic) word boundaries', the Hammock Principle (Van Zonneveld 1985); the mirror case infinitief has secondary stress on the final syllable; secondary stress is not weight-sensitive in Booij's analysis (p. 106, contra Kager 1989: identiteit, tuberculose, conservatief with initial secondary stress despite a closed second syllable); the extrametrical final syllable of olifant still receives secondary stress (p. 102); in compounds the first member's main stress becomes the compound stress, with Trochaic Reversal under clash (pp. 98-99).
new_statements.exceptions: Vowel-final words with antepenultimate stress (-ia, -io: aria, ratio) or final stress (French-type words: melodie, trofee, kado); -VC words with exceptional final stress (balkon, japon, kanon 'gun', karton) marked as exceptions to Extrametricality Rule (13); -VVC/-VCC words with exceptional non-final stress through lexically marked extrametricality (lichaam, hospitaal, andijvie, index, olifant, appendix, juffrouw, selderij); rule-predicted final extrametricality for the endings -ium, -i(C)o, -ina, -ika, -ier, -icus, -ia, -uwe (gymnasium, risico, pagina, Amerika, agrarier, medicus, malaria, Betuwe) giving antepenultimate stress (p. 103, (15)); -or words with penultimate stress even on an open penult (motor, condensator, alligator: final /r/ extrametrical, p. 103 (16)); more exceptions among native underived words than among non-native ones (p. 100).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Dutch main stress is computed from the right word edge over rimes assembled into feet: a final superheavy rime (VVC or VCC) forms its own foot and takes final stress (kostúum, cemént, garnizóen); a closed (VC) penult always takes stress (aórta, agénda, diléma incl. 'double spelling consonants'); with an open (VV) penult stress is either penultimate (diplóma, tornádo) or antepenultimate (pérgola, fárao), the antepenult being reached by marking the final rime stress-extrametrical (lexical marking); a final syllable with schwa can never bear main stress and forces main stress onto the immediately preceding syllable without exception (theáter, pantóffel, synagóge), which the authors derive by making the schwa appendix stress-extrametrical. Stress thus stays within the last three syllables and is sensitive to rime weight (VXC > VC > VV).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated as such; the paper builds w/s-labelled feet and a word tree (examples (46)-(47)) but makes no explicit statement about secondary-stress placement.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate stress usual before pre-final i (rádio, álibi, harmónica) but pre-final i stressed before schwa (machíne, pyramíde); a few irregular words with non-final stress despite a heavy final rime (áltaar, ámbacht, ólifant), handled by lexical stress-extrametricality of the final rime; stressed final VV rare, confined to recent loans (menú, buró); Faust the only known.aust word; pre-schwa stress said to be 'completely exceptionless'.
new_statements.identity_note: Standard Dutch (monomorphemic/underived words; authors at Utrecht); no particular dialect singled out.

tone_statements.quote: An autosegmental analysis consists of a string of low and high tones (L, H). Different kinds of tone can be distinguished on the basis of the place they take up in the larger phonological structure. Pitch accents are located in the accented syllables, of which every sentence or sentence fragment will have minimally one. The pitch accents of Dutch begin with a starred tone , and may have trailing tones after it. Thus, H* is a monotonal pitch accent, while H*L is a bitonal one. Boundary tones are located on the edges of the intonational phrase (IP). At the left edge, there must be either a %L or a %H, and at the right edge there may be either an L% or an H%. ... With the exception of the tone grammars of the Limburgisch and Rhenish dialects which have a lexical tone contrast (stoottoon vs sleeptoon, also Tonakzent/Accent 1 vs. Tonakzent/Accent 2) and which are for that reason tone languages , the tone grammars of the West Germanic languages have largely the same structure. In comparison with the tone grammars of other languages without lexical tone, the intonation of West Germanic languages is complex.

tone_statements.quote: The intonation system of Belgian Dutch is very similar to that of Netherlandic Dutch, i.e. pitch contours consist of combinations of rising and falling pitch movements between an upper and lower declination line. The most common pitch configuration consists of a prominence-lending rise–fall combination in the same syllable with a frequent variant in which the two prominence-lending movements are positioned on different syllables: they are connected by a stretch of high declination. Another frequent pitch configuration is a rise associated with continuation or question intonation.

tone_statements.quote: Dutch is a language with word stress. That is, one of the syllables of a word is perceived as the prominent one, the main stress of the word. ... The phoneticians Cohen, 't Hart, and Collier have shown that main stress is realized as a pitch movement on the relevant syllable, if the word in question bears a sentence accent. ... This does not mean that stress is to be equated with pitch movement. Stress is a more abstract property, which also manifests itself in vowel duration and (lack of) vowel reduction ... Note also that the location of stress plays a role in some morphological rules and lexical phonological rules, that is, at a level where pitch movements are not available yet.

sources.quote: In Dutch, most plural nouns end in either -en or -s, for example dier+en 'animals' or bakker+s 'bakers'. Generally, -en is used for nouns with a stressed final syllable, whereas -s is used for nouns with an unstressed final syllable. sources.quote: An autosegmental analysis consists of a string of low and high tones (L, H). Different kinds of tone can be distinguished on the basis of the place they take up in the larger phonological structure. Pitch accents are located in the accented syllables, of which every sentence or sentence fragment will have minimally one. The pitch accents of Dutch begin with a starred tone , and may have trailing tones after it. Thus, H* is a monotonal pitch accent, while H*L is a bitonal one. Boundary tones are located on the edges of the intonational phrase (IP). At the left edge, there must be either a %L or a %H, and at the right edge there may be either an L% or an H%. ... With the exception of the tone grammars of the Limburgisch and Rhenish dialects which have a lexical tone contrast (stoottoon vs sleeptoon, also Tonakzent/Accent 1 vs. Tonakzent/Accent 2) and which are for that reason tone languages , the tone grammars of the West Germanic languages have largely the same structure. In comparison with the tone grammars of other languages without lexical tone, the intonation of West Germanic languages is complex.

tone.quote: Main stress falls on the antepenult, the penult, or the final syllable of the word if the penult is open, and on the penult or the final syllable if the penult is closed. Minimal pairs are rare ... Largely depending on focus, intonational pitch accents will occur on the syllable with main stress of some words ... The realization of these pitch accents will extend as far as the next pitch accent or the single bar |, which marks off a minor intonational phrase. Utterance-final boundary tones may be added before the double bar |.
tone.summary: No lexical tone described. Word stress on one of the last three syllables, restricted by penult structure (open penult: antepenult/penult/final; closed penult: penult/final). Pitch accents are intonational, placed by focus on the main-stressed syllable of accented words; boundary tones at utterance end. Tone-bearing events are thus post-lexical only.

tone.quote: Dutch is a language with word stress. That is, one of the syllables of a word is perceived as the prominent one, the main stress of the word. ... The phoneticians Cohen, 't Hart, and Collier have shown that main stress is realized as a pitch movement on the relevant syllable, if the word in question bears a sentence accent. ... This does not mean that stress is to be equated with pitch movement. Stress is a more abstract property, which also manifests itself in vowel duration and (lack of) vowel reduction ... Note also that the location of stress plays a role in some morphological rules and lexical phonological rules, that is, at a level where pitch movements are not available yet.
